transcript.text: I need to flag something important before we go further. After the draft license was circulated, I pulled the latest patent-maintenance records. Right now, enforceable portfolio coverage for this license exists only in the United States and Germany — not worldwide as the draft implies. Additionally, the maintenance fee for US Patent 11-482901 is due in just 9 days. I haven't yet updated the patent schedule with these findings, but everyone should be aware that a 'worldwide exclusive license' would not currently have patent coverage outside the US and Germany, and we have an urgent maintenance deadline to address.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: I need to share critical information from a call I had with HelioGrid's commercial sponsor. The approved business term sheet — which HelioGrid has confirmed they will sign — permits exclusivity only for grid-scale battery storage applications, sets the royalty at exactly 6% of net sales, and prohibits sublicensing entirely. HelioGrid will not sign on the broader draft terms currently circulating. I have not yet entered these call terms into the deal tracker, which is why this hasn't been visible to the rest of you. This means the draft terms being discussed — 5% royalty, worldwide exclusivity, unrestricted sublicensing — are not aligned with what was actually approved and what HelioGrid will accept.
transcript.speaker: A3

transcript.text:
Thank you both. These are critical disclosures that fundamentally change the picture. Let me synthesize what we now know:

First, from Thomas: We cannot grant a 'worldwide exclusive license' in good faith because we only have enforceable patent coverage in the US and Germany. Any license must be scoped to those territories, or we risk granting rights we can't actually protect. And the US Patent 11-482901 maintenance fee due in 9 days is an urgent priority — if we let that lapse, we lose coverage in our largest market before this deal even closes.

Second, from Nadia: The draft terms circulating are misaligned with what was actually approved and what HelioGrid will sign. The real terms are: exclusivity limited to grid-scale battery storage applications only, 6% royalty (not 5%), and no sublicensing permitted.

So the path forward is clear. We should not approve the draft as written. Instead, we should authorize a license that: (1) covers only the US and Germany, matching our actual patent estate; (2) is exclusive only for grid-scale battery storage; (3) sets the royalty at 6%; and (4) prohibits sublicensing. We also need to authorize immediate payment of the US 11-482901 maintenance fee before the 9-day deadline.

Does anyone see issues with this approach before I formalize it?
transcript.speaker: A1
